# Why this package

A quantitative-genetic analysis needs four things at once: the marker
genotypes, the phenotypes, the pedigree, and where the markers sit on the
genome. Keeping them in four separate objects is where mistakes creep in, as
soon as one of them is filtered or reordered. Drop a marker from the genotype
matrix and the map no longer lines up; reorder the phenotypes and every
breeding value is attached to the wrong animal. Nothing warns you.

Bioconductor solved that problem generally with `SummarizedExperiment`, and
`BreedingExperiment` applies the solution to breeding data. It extends
`RangedSummarizedExperiment`, so markers are rows, individuals are columns,
and marker positions are a `GRanges`. Subsetting takes the genotypes, the
phenotypes, the marker coordinates and the pedigree with it. Everything you
already know about Bioconductor containers applies.

The relationship matrices are then methods on that container rather than
free-standing functions fed loose matrices:

* `Amatrix()`, the pedigree numerator relationship matrix;
* `Gmatrix()`, the genomic relationship matrix;
* `Dmatrix()`, the dominance relationship matrix;
* `Hmatrix()`, the single-step matrix combining pedigree and markers.

That last one is the reason the package exists. Real breeding programmes
genotype only part of the population, and single-step genomic prediction is
how the genotyped and ungenotyped parts are analysed together.

# What else is available

It is worth being specific about what this package adds, because the
individual matrices are not new.

On Bioconductor, relatedness is available from two directions, but never
both at once:

| Package | What it gives you |
| --- | --- |
| `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("SNPRelate")` | `snpgdsGRM()`, a genomic relationship matrix from GDS-backed genotypes, and IBD and PCA analyses. Scales far past this package, with no pedigree. |
| `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("GENESIS")` | PC-AiR and PC-Relate, kinship estimated from markers while adjusting for ancestry, plus mixed-model association testing. |
| `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("GeneticsPed")` | Pedigree classes, relationship and inbreeding coefficients. Pedigree only; its own description notes that it is not stable. |
| `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("Pedixplorer")` | `Pedigree` objects, kinship matrices and pedigree drawing, succeeding `kinship2`. Pedigree only. |
| `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("FamAgg")` | Pedigree handling and tests of familial aggregation of traits. Pedigree only. |

So Bioconductor can give you relationships from a pedigree, or relationships
from markers, but not a container that holds both kinds of data together and
not the single-step matrix that reconciles them.

On CRAN, `AGHmatrix` is the closest relative and in some ways goes further
than this package. It computes A, G, dominance and H matrices, it covers
autopolyploids as well as diploids, it offers several parameterisations of
each matrix, and it is compiled, so it is faster. What it does not do is hold
your data: it takes loose matrices and data frames and returns loose
matrices, leaving the genotypes, pedigree, phenotypes and map for you to keep
aligned. The differences worth knowing are:

* **Orientation.** `AGHmatrix::Gmatrix()` expects individuals in rows and
  markers in columns. This package follows the Bioconductor convention and
  puts markers in rows.
* **Single-step.** `AGHmatrix::Hmatrix()` takes an already-computed A and G
  and offers the Martini and Munoz methods. `Hmatrix()` here works from the
  object, and uses the tuning and blending described below.
* **Dominance.** `AGHmatrix` reaches dominance through
  `Gmatrix(method = "Vitezica")`; here it is `Dmatrix()`.
* **Names.** `AGHmatrix` also exports `Amatrix`, `Gmatrix` and `Hmatrix`, so
  loading both packages masks whichever was loaded first. Use
  `BreedingExperiment::Gmatrix()` if you need both in one session.

Choose `AGHmatrix` if you work on autopolyploids or want its alternative
parameterisations; choose `SNPRelate` if you have hundreds of thousands of
samples and no pedigree; choose this package if your data belong in a
Bioconductor container and you want the single-step matrix.

Two limitations are worth stating plainly. The relationship matrices are
dense base-R matrices, which suits thousands of individuals rather than
hundreds of thousands. And the package estimates no variance components and
fits no association tests: it produces the relationship structures, and a
solver consumes them, as shown at the end of this vignette.

# Installation

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("BreedingExperiment")
```

The development version lives on GitHub:

```{r install-dev, eval = FALSE}
BiocManager::install("mqfarooqi1/BreedingExperiment")
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(BreedingExperiment)
```

# The demonstration data

The package ships with `demoBreeding`, a simulated five-generation population
built to behave like a real programme rather than a textbook example.

```{r demo-data}
data(demoBreeding)
be <- demoBreeding
be
```

Read the last line carefully: the pedigree describes **180 individuals but only
120 were genotyped**. The two earliest generations were born before genotyping
began. That is the normal situation in a breeding programme, and it is the
reason `Hmatrix()` exists.

The data also carry the other awkward features of real records: a trait
measured on one sex only, a little missing genotype data, and unequal family
sizes because a few sires were used heavily.

```{r demo-features}
table(SummarizedExperiment::colData(be)$generation)
summary(SummarizedExperiment::colData(be)$yield)   # females only
```

If you would rather generate your own population, `simulateBreeding()` does
that.

The standard accessors work:

```{r accessors}
dim(be)
genotypes(be)[1:4, 1:5]
head(SummarizedExperiment::colData(be), 3)
head(pedigree(be), 3)
```

Because markers are genomic ranges, a data set can be cut down to a region:

```{r subset-region}
chr1 <- be[as.character(GenomicRanges::seqnames(
  SummarizedExperiment::rowRanges(be))) == "chr1", ]
dim(chr1)
```

# Building an object from your own data

Your own data goes in the same way:

```{r your-data, eval = FALSE}
be <- BreedingExperiment(
  genotypes  = dosage_matrix,          # markers x individuals, 0/1/2
  phenotypes = phenotype_data_frame,   # one row per individual
  pedigree   = pedigree_data_frame,    # id, sire, dam
  rowRanges  = marker_granges)         # optional, but worth having
```

Two habits are worth forming. Give `phenotypes` row names that are the
individual identifiers, and they will be matched by name rather than by
position; row names that do not match the genotype column names are an error
rather than something quietly overwritten. And pass real `rowRanges`
whenever you have them, because that is what makes a data set subsettable by
genomic region.

The pedigree may name ancestors that were never genotyped, which is exactly
what `Hmatrix()` needs. Parents that never appear in the `id` column are
added as founders, and unknown parents may be written `NA` or `0`.

# Quality control

```{r qc-summaries}
nrow(be)
summary(alleleFrequency(be)$callRate)
```

Take the marker summaries before imputing. `callRate` counts dosages that are
present, so after imputation it is 1 everywhere; observed `heterozygosity`,
by contrast, ignores imputed cells and is unaffected.

```{r qc}
be <- filterMarkers(be, min_maf = 0.05, min_call_rate = 0.9)
be <- imputeMarkers(be)
nrow(be)
head(alleleFrequency(be), 3)
```

## Choosing the thresholds

`min_maf` and `min_call_rate` are judgement calls, not constants of nature.
Common starting points are a minor allele frequency between 0.01 and 0.05 and
a call rate between 0.90 and 0.95. Raise `min_maf` when the panel is large
and the sample small, because an allele seen in one or two individuals says
almost nothing about relationships while still adding noise; lower it when
rare variants are the point of the study. Filter before imputing, so that
imputation is not asked to rescue markers that should simply be discarded.

How much this matters is worth checking rather than assuming:

```{r qc-sensitivity}
# on the unfiltered data, so that every threshold has markers to remove
round(t(vapply(c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.20), function(m) {
  G <- Gmatrix(demoBreeding, min_maf = m)
  c(min_maf = m, mean_diagonal = mean(diag(G)),
    sd_offdiagonal = stats::sd(G[upper.tri(G)]))
}, numeric(3))), 3)
```

`imputeMarkers()` fills missing dosages with twice the allele frequency and
records which cells it filled in an `imputed` assay, carried through
subsetting with everything else:

```{r imputed-assay}
SummarizedExperiment::assayNames(be)
mean(SummarizedExperiment::assay(be, "imputed"))   # proportion imputed
```

That is adequate for the low missingness left after filtering. For anything
more, impute with dedicated software and pass the expected dosages in
directly; the container accepts values between 0 and 2.

# Relationships from the pedigree

`Amatrix()` builds the numerator relationship matrix. Its entries are the
familiar textbook values: one half between parent and offspring, one quarter
between grandparent and grandchild.

```{r amatrix}
A <- Amatrix(be)
round(A[1:5, 1:5], 3)
```

The diagonal carries inbreeding:

```{r inbreeding}
summary(inbreeding(be))
```

# Relationships from the markers

`Gmatrix()` is the genomic relationship matrix. It measures what actually
happened rather than what was expected: two full sibs have a pedigree
relationship of exactly 0.5, but their genomic relationship varies around it,
because Mendelian sampling gave them different halves of their parents.

```{r gmatrix}
G <- Gmatrix(be)
round(G[1:5, 1:5], 3)
```

The two agree in the aggregate, which is a useful sanity check on any data set:

```{r ag-agreement}
gen <- colnames(be)
A22 <- A[gen, gen]
cor(A22[upper.tri(A22)], G[upper.tri(G)])
```

```{r ag-plot, fig.wide = TRUE, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Pedigree and genomic relationships for the same pairs of individuals. The pedigree gives a few discrete values; the markers spread each of them out, and that spread is the Mendelian sampling a pedigree cannot see."}
plot(A22[upper.tri(A22)], G[upper.tri(G)], pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
     col = grDevices::adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.3),
     xlab = "pedigree relationship", ylab = "genomic relationship")
abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
```

`Dmatrix()` gives the dominance relationships, orthogonal to the additive
ones, for models that separate the two:

```{r dmatrix}
D <- Dmatrix(be)
round(D[1:4, 1:4], 3)
```

# Combining both: the single-step matrix

Using only `G` discards every ungenotyped relative. Using only `A` discards
the markers. `Hmatrix()` keeps both, and covers every individual in the
pedigree:

```{r hmatrix}
H <- Hmatrix(be, blend = 0.05)
dim(H)
length(attr(H, "genotyped"))
```

The genotyped block comes from the markers, the ungenotyped block from the
pedigree corrected by what the markers say about genotyped relatives, and the
off-diagonal blocks connect them. Two checks confirm the behaviour: blending
entirely towards the pedigree returns `A22`, and the result stays positive
definite.

```{r hmatrix-checks}
H1 <- Hmatrix(be, blend = 1, tune = FALSE)
max(abs(H1[gen, gen] - A22))
min(eigen(H, only.values = TRUE)$values) > 0
```

## Choosing blend and tune

Leave `tune = TRUE` unless you have already put `G` on the scale of `A22`
yourself. Untuned, the two matrices usually disagree about the average level
of relationship, and that disagreement is passed straight into the
ungenotyped block, where it appears as breeding values biased between the
genotyped and ungenotyped groups.

`blend` has two jobs. A small weight on `A22` makes the genotyped block
invertible, which matters whenever there are fewer markers than genotyped
individuals, and it pulls the markers back towards the pedigree where the
marker estimate is noisy. Values between 0.01 and 0.10 are usual and 0.05 is
a reasonable default: use 0.05 to 0.10 for a small marker panel and 0.01 to
0.02 for a dense one on many individuals. `blend = 0` keeps `G` as it is and
will fail if `G` is singular; `blend = 1` discards the markers altogether.

With 801 markers on 120 individuals the choice makes very little difference
here, which is itself the point: blending matters most when `G` is close to
singular.

```{r blend-sweep}
vapply(c(0.02, 0.05, 0.20), function(b) {
  Hb <- Hmatrix(be, blend = b)
  min(eigen(Hb, only.values = TRUE)$values)
}, numeric(1))
```

# A complete example: single-step BLUP

The matrices are not the end of an analysis, so here is what you do with one.
These are Henderson's mixed model equations for a single random genetic
effect,
$$y = Xb + Zu + e, \qquad u \sim N(0, K\sigma^2_u), \qquad
  e \sim N(0, I\sigma^2_e),$$
solved directly with $\lambda = \sigma^2_e / \sigma^2_u$:
$$\begin{bmatrix} X'X & X'Z \\ Z'X & Z'Z + K^{-1}\lambda \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix} b \\ u \end{bmatrix} =
  \begin{bmatrix} X'y \\ Z'y \end{bmatrix}.$$

Put `H` in for $K$ and the solution covers every individual in the pedigree,
genotyped or not. The validation is the one a breeder actually cares about:
hide the records of the youngest generation, predict their breeding values
from their parents and their markers, and see how well the predictions
correlate with the truth that the simulation knows.

```{r blup-setup}
ph  <- SummarizedExperiment::colData(be)
ids <- rownames(H)

train  <- ph$generation != 5                 # records we are allowed to use
target <- colnames(be)[ph$generation == 5]   # the ones we must predict
y <- ph$stature[train]

X <- matrix(1, length(y), 1)                 # an intercept only
Z <- matrix(0, length(y), length(ids))       # records to individuals
Z[cbind(seq_along(y), match(colnames(be)[train], ids))] <- 1
c(records = length(y), predicted = length(target))
```

```{r blup-solve}
blup <- function(K, h2) {
  lambda <- (1 - h2) / h2
  lhs <- rbind(cbind(crossprod(X),    crossprod(X, Z)),
               cbind(crossprod(Z, X), crossprod(Z) + solve(K) * lambda))
  rhs <- rbind(crossprod(X, y), crossprod(Z, y))
  stats::setNames(solve(lhs, rhs)[-1, 1], ids)
}

ebv_pedigree   <- blup(A[ids, ids], h2 = 0.6)
ebv_singlestep <- blup(H,           h2 = 0.6)
```

`stature` was simulated with a heritability of 0.6, which is the value used
here. In a real analysis the variance components are estimated, by REML in a
package such as `sommer`, `rrBLUP`, `BGLR` or `lme4qtl`, or by standalone
software such as ASReml or BLUPF90; all of them accept a relationship matrix
or its inverse, which is what this package produces.

```{r blup-accuracy}
true <- stats::setNames(ph$trueBV_stature, colnames(be))
round(c(pedigree   = cor(ebv_pedigree[target],   true[target]),
        singlestep = cor(ebv_singlestep[target], true[target])), 3)
```

Adding the markers raises the correlation with the true breeding values of
the unrecorded generation. The gain is real but modest, and that is honest
for this data set: the simulated pedigree is complete and error-free, which
is the situation in which a pedigree-only analysis does best. The advantage
of single-step grows as pedigrees become incomplete and as more records
accumulate on ungenotyped relatives.

```{r blup-plot, fig.wide = TRUE, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Predicted against true breeding values for the youngest generation, whose records were withheld. Adding marker information tightens the relationship."}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (nm in c("pedigree", "singlestep")) {
  e <- if (nm == "pedigree") ebv_pedigree else ebv_singlestep
  plot(true[target], e[target], pch = 16, col = "steelblue",
       xlab = "true breeding value", ylab = "predicted",
       main = sprintf("%s (r = %.3f)", nm, cor(e[target], true[target])))
  abline(lm(e[target] ~ true[target]), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
}
par(op)
```

The other half of what `H` buys you is easy to miss: the 60 ungenotyped
ancestors get predictions too, on the same scale, from one solve.

```{r blup-ungenotyped}
ungenotyped <- setdiff(ids, attr(H, "genotyped"))
length(ungenotyped)
summary(ebv_singlestep[ungenotyped])
```
